title: A home-based exercise program for children with congenital heart disease following interventional cardiac catheterization: study protocol for a randomized controlled trial

content: Significant improvements in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) outcomes have been realized since the implementation of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and regionalized systems of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) care, with in-hospital mortality rates of less than 5% in the contemporary era. AMI complicated by cardiogenic shock (CS), however, continues to be plagued with high rates of morbidity and mortality which have remained in excess of 40% since the seminal Should We Revascularize Occluded Arteries in Cardiogenic Shock (SHOCK) trial in 1999. Several factors may account for these suboptimal outcomes: 1) Vasopressors and inotropes are cardiotoxic as they increase myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2); 2) Practice pattern variations persist in the utilization of pulmonary arterial catheters (PAC) despite the fact that they have not been prospectively studied in shock care, and there is increasing body of evidence supporting the merits of invasive hemodynamic monitoring in CS; 3) Clinical gaps in knowledge exist regarding optimal revascularization strategies in this patient population; 4) Significant disparities remain in the utilization rates and clinical outcomes associated with mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices. To address the current state of clinical equipoise in shock care, we review the pathophysiology and evolving definitions of AMI-CS, we review the literature and present contemporary best practices for the management of this challenging syndrome in the cardiac catheterization laboratories. Initially coined a "downward spiral" by Hollenberg in 1999, the pathophysiologic paradigm of AMI-CS is one in which acute coronary thrombosis results in severely impaired contractility of the subtended myocardial mass with concomitant systolic and diastolic pump failure, triggering a deleterious and self-perpetuating spiral of systemic hypoperfusion, compensatory vasoconstriction, augmented ventricular diastolic pressures with refractory coronary ischemia, pulmonary congestion, increased biventricular afterload, lactic acidosis and ultimately death. Nearly 20% of patients may also develop a systemic inflammatory response syndrome due to increased production of nitric oxide, peroxynitrite, interleukins and other inflammatory mediators, which have negative inotropic effects and induce systemic vasoplegia. While coronary reperfusion is the only therapy proven to be effective in short-circuiting this maladaptive cascade, it can also induce myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury (IRI), a malignant byproduct of regenerated adenosine triphosphate causing myofibrillar hypercontractility due to intracellular calcium overload following the opening of mitochondrial permeability transition pores and increased production of reactive oxygen species, and resulting in heightened MVO2, microvascular obstruction and cellular death. It is reported that IRI may account for up to 50% of post-infarct scar, a powerful predictor of all-cause mortality and heart failure rehospitalizations during the first year following AMI. To date, a number of clinical studies evaluating pharmacologic and mechanical cardioprotective strategies in AMI without CS have been performed and the results have been mixed. Nevertheless, there has been a resurgence of interest in the field of ischemic pre- conditioning with ongoing research evaluating the utility of LV unloading using axial flow MCS devices prior to reperfusion in patients with anterior STEMI and AMI-CS. Historically, the espoused definition of CS has been a state of volume unresponsive hemodynamic compromise and frank circulatory collapse due to primary cardiac dysfunction stemming from a multitude of etiologies, to include diseases of the myocardium, pericardium, valvular heart disease or primary arrhythmias. While initial clinical profiling of CS was predicated on invasive hemodynamic assessments to stratify risk, contemporary clinical trials and guidelines have differed with regards to criteria needed to diagnose CS. Subsequent analyses have further defined the classification of CS phenotypes as left ventricular (LV) dominant, right ventricular (RV) dominant and biventricular (BiV) CS. Hemodynamic manifestations of RV-dominant CS include elevated central venous pressure (CVP), low-normal pulmonary arterial pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), CVP/PCWP >0.86 and cardiac index < 1.8 L/min/m2 . Clinical severity of CS in these patients is determined in part by the degree of LV dysfunction, given that the interventricular septum is responsible for up to 40% of RV contractile force. A recent post-hoc analysis demonstrated that 38% of the initial SHOCK trial had RV dysfunction, and despite a younger patient population with a lower burden of multi-vessel disease, they had similarly high mortality as patients with LV Shock (53.1% vs. 60.8%; p=0.296). Elevated BiV filling pressures can be seen in up to 40% of CS patients and is associated with increased risk for end organ congestion and mortality. Lastly, there is the phenotype of pre-shock, a high risk cohort of patients, in whom a systolic blood pressure >90 mm Hg is maintained by way of systemic vasoconstriction as a mechanism to compensate for end organ hypoperfusion. In 2019, the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) put forth a five stage A-E classification system for CS to serve as a lingua franca for more consistent classification and communication of disease severity (Fig. 1). Each stage is characterized by a stock phrase that is an amalgamation of three of clinical domains: bedside physical exam findings, laboratory biomarkers and invasive hemodynamics. To date, the SCAI nomenclature has been retrospectively validated, with each stage shown to be associated with in-hospital mortality and 30-day outcomes. Contemporary analyses of North American and European registries estimate the prevalence of CS complicating AMI as 5-12%. In addition, the patient population is increasingly complex with a heightened burden of "hemo-metabolic" acuity and multi-organ system failure. More than 50% will present with cardiac arrest; greater than 80% will require mechanical ventilation; and nearly 35% will develop acute kidney injury. In addition, mechanical complications, such as free wall rupture, ventricular septal defect and papillary muscle rupture, may be seen in up to 0.3% of AMI's, with more than 50% progressing to CS with in-hospital rates of at least 40%. Despite advances in early reperfusion, there remain numerous challenges that contribute to the disparities in clinical outcomes in patients with AMI-CS. Up to 50% will present to lower volume PCI centers (<500/year), a notable finding given the documented relationship between clinical volume and institutional competencies in optimizing outcomes. In addition, a recent subgroup analysis of the American Heart Association Mission: Lifeline STEMI Systems Accelerator Initiative reported that less than 40% of patients with STEMI complicated by CS will achieve the guideline-directed first medical contact-to-device time of <=90 minutes, a powerful predictor of clinical outcomes, as every 10 minute treatment delay may result in up to 3 deaths in 100 PCI-treated patients. Lastly, more than 20% of patients will have a major bleeding complication, an independent predictor of mortality in AMI-CS. Given these considerations, a review of contemporary strategies in the cardiac catheterization laboratories to improve outcomes in this high-risk cohort is in order. We will focus on five clinical domains: vascular access, anti-thrombotic pharmacotherapy, revascularization strategies, invasive hemodynamics, and MCS. We will also address the management of cardiac arrest complicating AMI-CS. As many as 80% of patients with AMI-CS may develop acute hypoxemic respiratory failure either at index clinical presentation or during the hospital course as a consequence of their illness. This is primarily due to elevations in end diastolic filling pressures resulting in pulmonary edema, diminished gas exchange and metabolic acidosis. A recent analysis of 439,436 admissions for AMI-CS from the National Inpatient Sample noted that 57% of patients were diagnosed with acute respiratory failure, with a greater than 10-fold rise in the need for mechanical ventilation over a 14 year period. CS complicated by acute respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation had a significantly higher in-hospital mortality compared to CS without acute respiratory failure (49.4% vs. 28.1%; OR 2.50 [95% CI 2.47-2.54]; p< 0.001). Understanding the interactions between positive pressure ventilation and right and left ventricular physiology is key to the management of respiratory failure in AMI-CS. In patients with left ventricular-dominant CS, positive end-expiratory pressure has favorable effects on myocardial function by reducing left ventricular preload and afterload through attenuation of transthoracic and transpulmonary pressures and interstitial edema. The net effect is reductions in pulmonary vasoconstriction, hypercarbia, mitral regurgitation and myocardial oxygen demand. In patients with right ventricular dominant-CS, however, excessive positive end-expiratory pressure may have deleterious hemodynamic effects, as it can reduce venous return and increase pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in right ventricular dilation, impaired left ventricular diastolic filling, and thus diminished cardiac output. Given the time-dependent benefit of respiratory stabilization and the reported associations between delays in mechanical ventilation and short-term outcomes in CS, strong consideration should be given to early intubation and optimization of acid-base status prior to coronary angiography and revascularization in patients with AMI-CS. Since the initial case series documenting the feasibility of transradial access (TRA) for PCI by Ferdinand Kiemeneij in 1993, clinical trials have demonstrated the merits of TRA in reducing the risk of major bleeding, vascular complications, and major adverse cardiovascular events compared to the femoral approach. This body of evidence has been borne out by the increased uptake of TRA for primary PCI in STEMI in the United States, from 2% in 2009 to 23% in 2015. Moreover, the 2018 scientific statement by the American Heart Association supported a "radial-first" strategy for the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome. Though uncommon, vascular access site complications such as spasm, hematoma, arteriovenous fistulae and radial artery occlusions may occur in up to 10% of TRA cases, thus precluding the use of the radial artery as a conduit for future cardiac catheterizations or coronary artery bypass grafting. Recently, distal transradial access (dTRA) in the dorsum of the hand beneath the tendon of the extensor pollicis longus and between the bases of the first and second metacarpals, has been identified as an alternative site for TRA. The rationale for dTRA is its anatomic location distal to the palmar carpal arterial arch where collateral circulations exist, thus attenuating the risk for forearm vessel occlusion. While patients with AMI-CS were either excluded or underrepresented in many of the clinical trials, observational studies do support utilization of the radial artery in AMI-CS. Two important factors, however, must be taken into consideration: 1) CS is an established independent predictor of TRA failure, as these patients are often vasoconstricted and on temporizing vasopressor; and 2) Despite an increase in TRA uptake, vascular complications are also on the rise, due to the increasing need for large bore secondary femoral access to facilitate MCS. While clinical trials have demonstrated that ultrasound guidance can improve first pass success rates during transradial and transfemoral access and decrease bleeding events, it remains underutilized in contemporary practice, particularly in AMI-CS. Therefore, concerted efforts should be made to incorporate standardized vascular access protocols in the care of AMI-CS patients which emphasize: 1) ultrasound guided transradial access for coronary angiography and PCI; and 2) if radial (or ulnar access) is not feasible or secondary femoral access is required, best practices should be employed which incorporate ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance, use of micro-puncture needles, and dedicated hemostasis protocols. The foundation of contemporary antithrombotic therapy in patients with AMI undergoing PCI is dual antiplatelet inhibition, with aspirin and an oral P2Y12 inhibitor, in addition to periprocedural antithrombin administration. Ticagrelor and prasugrel both affect rapid and consistent platelet inhibition and are preferred over clopidogrel given their superior clinical efficacy. Patients with CS, however, were excluded from these studies. Furthermore, CS is a major predictor of stent thrombosis. The physiologic milieu of the shock state also poses significant challenges which confound the periprocedural risks for bleeding in addition to thrombosis through a combination of factors: 1) microcirculatory dysfunction; 2) altered drug pharmacokinetics, particularly delayed cytochrome-P450-dependent activation of clopidogrel due to hepatic edema and delayed gastrointestinal absorption in the setting of opioid administration; 3) platelet dysfunction stemming from targeted temperature management and potential renal failure; and 4) enhanced risk for vascular complications from large bore access. Limited data exist regarding the clinical efficacy and safety profiles of the various antithrombotic agents in AMI-CS, and so consensus recommendations have been extrapolated from more stable, non-CS AMI patients. The various studies of anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapies in AMI-CS are outlined in (Supplementary Table ). To date, post-hoc analyses of randomized controlled trials and observational studies have not demonstrated increased bleeding risk with the newer generation P2Y12 inhibitors prasugrel and ticagrelor in AMI-CS, thus rendering them the oral antiplatelet agents of choice, preferably in crushed formulation given data demonstrating faster drug absorption and more potent platelet inhibition compared to whole tablet ingestion. A non-randomized observational subgroup analysis of the Intraaortic Balloon Pump in Cardiogenic Shock II (IABP -SHOCK II) trial did not demonstrate a difference in the adjusted rate of mortality (HR: 0.83, 95% CI: 0.59-1.19, p=0.31) or GUSTO bleeding (HR: 0.91, 95% CI:0.55-1.5, p=0.7) between patients with AMI-CS treated with prasugrel/ticagrelor or clopidogrel. A retrospective analysis of 145 patients from the ISAR-SHOCK registry demonstrated reduced all-cause mortality (30% vs. 50.5%, HR:0.51, 95% CI [0.29-0.92], p=0.025), and ADP-induced platelet aggregation in AMI-CS patients treated with prasugrel compared to clopidogrel without significant differences in myocardial infarction or TIMI major bleeding. The intravenous P2Y12 inhibitor cangrelor which has been shown to be clinically superior to clopidogrel in reducing the endpoints of death, MI, ischemia-driven revascularization and acute stent thrombosis in patients with stable angina and acute coronary syndrome, may be an attractive agent in bridging the gap in platelet inhibition in AMI-CS when oral agents may have limited bioavailability. It is unique pharmacodynamically for its rapid onset of action with the ability to achieve steady-date concentration within 2 minutes of infusion, 100% bioavailability as it does not require metabolic activation, and its short half -life of 3-6 minutes with rapid offset of action. It has been studied in resuscitated patients following cardiac arrest and shown to effect greater platelet inhibition compared to oral P2Y12 inhibitors without significant increases in major bleeding. The Dual Antiplatelet Therapy for Shock Patients with Acute Myocardial Infarction trial (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI) (ClinicalTrial.gov:NCR03551964) is an ongoing multicenter randomized study which will compare the clinical efficacy of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in AMI-CS, and it will examine the combined endpoint of death, MI and stroke at 30 days. Thus far, only been one randomized controlled trial has examined glycoprotein IIbIIIa inhibition in AMI-CS and in a sample of 80 patients, there was no difference in the 30-day combined outcome of death, re-infarction, stroke and new severe renal failure in patients who received routine up-stream abciximab prior to primary PCI. Current revascularization guidelines afford intravenous glycoprotein IIbIIIa administration a class IIa recommendation in AMI care as a bailout strategy in the event of high coronary thrombus burden, no-reflow or acute vessel closure during PCI. Randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of various anticoagulants in AMI-CS are similarly lacking. While low molecular weight heparin and direct thrombin inhibitors may have more predictable pharmacokinetics compared to unfractionated heparin, impaired renal and hepatic function as well as subcutaneous absorption may hamper their efficacy in AMI-CS. To date, two retrospective observational studies comparing bivalirudin and unfractionated heparin in AMI-CS have had conflicting results, with the most recent study of 91 patients from the University of Ottawa Heart Institute demonstrating no difference in the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction and stroke (44% of patients receiving bivalirudin vs. 58% of patients treated with heparin alone; OR 0.76, CI 0.36-1.60, p=0.47) or major bleeding (18% vs. 19%, p=0.87). However, there was nearly a 7 fold increased risk of stent thrombosis and re-infarction with bivalirudin. The American Heart Association position statement on CS and European guidelines currently favor unfractionated heparin as the anticoagulant of choice in AMI-CS given its rapid offset and reversibility. Since the publication of the SHOCK trial, early revascularization has been the standard of care in AMI-CS management . Greater than 70% of patients with AMI-CS, however, will have multi-vessel coronary artery disease, an independent predictor of mortality in this patient high-risk cohort. While the benefits of complete coronary revascularization in hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI are well established, clinical gaps in knowledge remain regarding best practices for the treatment of non-infarct related lesions in AMI-CS. Notwithstanding the survival benefit and durability of surgical revascularization in patients with multi-vessel disease and left ventricular systolic dysfunction, data from observational studies and contemporary practice suggest that <7% of patients with AMI-CS will undergo coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) given their heightened operative risk for morbidity and mortality . While initial post-hoc analyses from the SHOCK trial demonstrated increased mortality with ad-hoc multi-vessel PCI (adjusted HR 2.75; 95% CI 1.05-7.25; p=0.04), subsequent observational studies have had conflicting findings (Supplementary Table ). The Culprit Lesion Only PCI versus Multi-vessel PCI in Cardiogenic Shock (CULPRIT-SHOCK) trial is the only randomized controlled trial to address this issue and it demonstrated that a strategy of culprit-lesion PCI (with an option for staged revascularization) was clinically superior to ad-hoc multi-vessel PCI by affording a significant reduction in the primary end-point of 30-day mortality or renal replacement therapy (45.9% vs. 55.4%; relative risk, 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.71-0.96; p=0.01) . The primary outcome endured through one year follow-up, but there were higher rates of heart failure re-hospitalizations and repeat revascularizations in the culprit-lesion PCI arm in the landmark analysis. This study has been critiqued as only 28% of patients were supported with a hemodynamic assist device, whereas previous post-hoc analytic findings have suggested improved procedural hemodynamics and the ability to provide complete revascularization with axial flow support platform Impella (Abiomed, Danvers, MA) in patients with left ventricular dysfunction. In addition, revascularization of all vessels with >70% luminal stenosis was recommended in the multi-vessel group, including chronic total occlusions, which comprised 24% of the cohort. To date, a strategy of ad-hoc revascularization of chronic total occlusions following primary PCI for STEMI has not been shown to improve left ventricular geometry or function. Recently investigators from the National Cardiogenic Shock Initiative (NCSI), a multi-center prospective registry employing standardized protocols for AMI-CS management including early invasive hemodynamics and left ventricular unloading with Impella prior to PCI, demonstrated in a sub-study analysis of 300 patients that there were no significant differences in-hospital mortality, acute kidney injury and hospital length of stay between culprit and multi-vessel revascularization . Given the observational nature of this study, further research is needed with randomized controlled experiments to determine whether ischemic preconditioning with mechanical LV unloading can modulate the risks for short term mortality and acute kidney injury in patients with AMI-CS undergoing multi-vessel PCI. The 2019 European guidelines downgraded ad-hoc multi-vessel PCI in AMI-CS from a Class IIa (Level of Evidence C) to a Class III (Level of Evidence of B) recommendations following the results of the CULPRIT-SHOCK study. The US Appropriateness Use Criteria, however, state that non-infarct vessel PCI may be considered in selected patients with AMI, if CS persists following culprit vessel revascularization []. While second generation drug eluting stents have been shown to exhibit greater efficacy with lower rates of target vessel revascularization and very late stent thrombosis compared to bare metal and first generation stents in acute coronary syndromes, patients with AMI-CS have either been excluded or under-represented in these studies, and so clinical data with regards to stent platform utilization in AMI-CS has been limited to retrospective observational registries. The largest population database to evaluate drug and bare metal stents in patients with AMI-CS was published in Taiwan from the National Health Insurance Research Database (n=3,051), and it demonstrated over a mean follow-up period of 1.35 years (SD = 1.42 years), the use of DES was associated with lower rates of death, AMI, stroke and coronary revascularization, compared to BMS [56.1% vs. 66.2%, HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.67-0.81). Post-hoc analysis from the Intra-aortic Balloon Pump in Cardiogenic Shock II (IABP-SHOCK II) trial, however, did not demonstrate any difference in 1-year mortality or re-infarction between drug and bare metal stents following adjustment for baseline patient characteristics. Traditionally, angiographic and clinical predictors of in-stent restenosis such as lesion length and complexity, minimal luminal diameter, diabetes, renal insufficiency and duration of dual antiplatelet therapy have guided clinical decision making in stent platform selection. However, given the technologic and pharmacokinetic improvements in newer-generation thin strutted DES as well as emerging data regarding the decremental obligation for dual antithrombotic therapy in patients at high risk for bleeding complications following PCI, drug eluting stents should be the preferred stent platform during revascularization in AMI-CS. Short-term MCS devices are increasingly utilized in AMI-CS to enhance hemodynamic performance, to halt the deleterious cycles of impaired cardiac output and end organ malperfusion, and to facilitate myocardial recovery or serve as a bridge to advanced heart failure therapies. An analysis of the National Inpatient Sample from 2012 to 2015 demonstrated a nearly a 1.5 fold increase in the use of Impella and veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) in the management of AMI-CS, while uptake of the intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) declined by almost 25% during that time. Nevertheless, routine employment of temporary circulatory support remains controversial and current guidelines provide a Class IIb level of evidence of C recommendation in the deployment of these devices in all-comer AMI-CS patients given the paucity of randomized controlled trials supporting their use. Potential benefits of these devices include enhanced circulatory support to maintain a viable mean arterial blood pressure, attenuation of stroke work and myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO2), augmentation of coronary and end organ perfusion, and reduction in infarct size. Device selection should be guided by the mechanism of cardiac failure (LV, RV or BiV CS), operator and institutional experience with device management and an innate understanding of how each device platform modulates pressure-volume interactions (Fig. 2). The hemodynamic complexities of CS and the challenges associated with clinical assessment of patients with advanced heart failure highlight the importance of objective data to guide clinical decision-making. Notwithstanding the absence of clinical benefit in all-comer heart failure patients and its falling out of favor in clinical practice, there is growing evidence from US shock center registries that selective MCS utilization predicated on serial hemometabolic parameters, including cardiac power output, pulmonary arterial pulsatility index and lactates may not only facilitate earlier shock recognition and application of MCS strategies tailored to the individual CS phenotype but also may be associated with improved outcomes. Based on these findings, there are increasing calls to incorporate early utilization of the pulmonary arterial catheter in contemporary CS management. Lastly, given the inherently resource intensive nature of MCS management, US and European guidelines recommend that the care of patients with AMI-CS requiring temporary circulatory support be confined to specialized Level 1 centers with dedicated cardiac intensive care units and Shock Teams comprised of members from interventional cardiology, cardiac surgery, advanced heart failure and cardiac critical care capable of guiding MCS escalation and weaning strategies in addition to providing full spectrum multi-organ system care (Fig. 3). The IABP provides counterpulsation through synchronized diastolic inflation and systolic deflation in the descending thoracoabdominal aorta. The net hemodynamic effect is a mild increase (0.3-0.5 L/min) in cardiac output with enhanced coronary perfusion and reduced ventricular afterload, although these effects are markedly diminished in the absence of native pulsation and electrical stability. Despite these purported benefits, The IABP-SHOCK II study, a multi-center randomized controlled trial of 600 patients with AMI-CS, demonstrated no differences in 30-day mortality (relative risk with IABP, 0.96; 95% CI 0.79-1.17; p=0.69), time to hemodynamic stabilization, length of intensive care unit stay, duration of vasopressors, major bleeding or stroke between IABP and medical therapy following revascularization . The absence of mortality benefit endured at six years follow-up between the two arms (relative risk with IABP, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.88-1.11; p=0.98), with further equipoise seen in rates of recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke, repeat revascularization as well as quality of life. Following the results of this trial, US and European guidelines downgraded the empiric use of IABP in AMI-CS to IIa level of evidence of B and Class III level of evidence B, respectively. The device may still have a role, however, following mechanical complications of AMI, such as ventricular septal defects or papillary muscle rupture with severe mitral regurgitation. Contraindications to IABP include severe aortic insufficiency, aortic dissection and peripheral arterial disease. The Impella percutaneous ventricular assist device is a microaxial flow pump capable of providing up to 5 L of cardiac output. It offers circulatory support and reduces cardiac stroke work by directly unloading the LV. It received US and Food Drug Administration 510 (k) approval in 2008 for high-risk PCI, with an expanded indication for CS in April 2016. Despite the capability to provide enhanced hemodynamic support, two RCT's have failed to demonstrate a mortality benefit with Impella compared to the IABP in AMI-CS. In addition, recent observational data from the Premier Healthcare Database examining unselected patients undergoing PCI with MCS suggested that there is greater than 5 fold variation in Impella utilization across hospitals, with >2.5 fold variation in bleeding outcomes and increased incidence of death (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI, 1.13-1.36) and stroke (odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI, 1.18-1.53). Similarly, an analysis of the American College of Cardiology's CathPCI and Chest Pain-MI registries demonstrated in a propensity matched analysis of patients undergoing PCI for AMI-CS higher risks of in-hospital death (45% vs. 34.1%, absolute risk difference 10.9% [95% CI, 7.6-14.2, p <0.001]) and in-hospital major bleeding (31.3% vs. 16%, absolute risk difference 15.4% [95% CI, 12.5-18.2, p <0.001]) with Impella compared to IABP, findings that were consistent regardless of whether the Impella was implanted pre- or post-PCI. A recent retrospective observational analysis of 166 consecutive IABP-SHOCK II eligible patients in 4 high volume German and Danish shock centers, however, demonstrated significantly lower 30-day mortality in AMI-CS patients supported with Impella as compared to risk predicted by the validated CardShock score [predicted 77% vs. 51% observed, p=0.0011, OR 0.30, 95% CI (0.15-0.61)]. Interestingly, the authors noted a mortality reduction when the device was implanted pre-PCI as compared to post-PCI (28% vs. 51%; p=0.025). The ongoing Danish-German CS (DanGer) CS trial (NCT01633502), a prospective, randomized, study aimed at examining whether early treatment with Impella CP may improve all-cause mortality in select AMI-CS patients, will provide further insight into the potential utility of this device when implemented using standardized protocols. Contraindications to Impella include critical aortic stenosis, presence of mechanical aortic valve prosthesis, severe aortic insufficiency, left ventricular mural thrombus and active bleeding. TandemHeart is a percutaneously inserted centrifugal-flow MCS device that pumps blood extracorporeally from the left atrium to the iliofemoral circuit via a transseptally placed left atrial (LA) cannula. Redirection of blood from the LA reduces LV preload, wall stress and MVO2 while augmenting cardiac output and mean arterial pressure. An RCT evaluating 42 patients presenting within 24 hours of CS demonstrated improved greater reductions in PCWP and increase with TandemHeart compared to IABP, but no difference in 30-day survival was noted. Since its inception in the 1970's as a means to aggressively support patients with fulminant respiratory failure, there has been nearly a 1200% increase in VA-ECMO utilization over the last decade nationwide as its indication has expanded to frank circulatory collapse and CS due to a multitude of etiologies, including but not limited to AMI, acute on chronic systolic heart failure, post-cardiotomy state, cardiac arrest, acute myocarditis, allograft rejection and acute pulmonary embolism with right ventricular failure. With the updated United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) donor allocation system in 2018, which prioritizes patients on temporary circulatory support for expedited allograft transplantation, further growth in VA-ECMO utilization is expected. Peripheral ECMO can be rapidly deployed via a venous cannula inserted in the femoral vein to achieve right atrial drainage with retrograde flow into the iliofemoral circuit to sustain mean arterial pressure and end-organ perfusion. An antegrade distal perfusion catheter may also be placed into the ipsilateral superficial femoral artery to minimize the risk for limb ischemia and vascular complications. A key limitation to prolonged support with VA-ECMO is increased ventricular afterload, resulting in augmented left ventricular end-diastolic pressures and wall stress, heightened MVO2 coronary ischemia, aortic and mitral incompetence and refractory pulmonary edema. A number of LV venting strategies have been proposed to mitigate this risk, including inotropic therapy, IABP, Impella, atrial septostomy and LV apical cannulation, although the optimal timing and mode of venting remain unclear. Due to large cannula sizes and the need for systemic anticoagulation, rates of ECMO-associated complications are not insignificant, and they contribute to the high mortality rates seen in patients supported with this device. A meta-analysis of 20 studies comprised of 1866 patients supported with VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest reported 17% rate of lower extremity ischemia, 6% stroke, 46% renal failure requiring dialysis and 41% rate of significant bleeding. Contraindications to VA-ECMO include irreversible non-cardiac organ failure, which would otherwise limit life expectancy (metastatic malignancy, anoxic brain injury), advanced liver disease with coexistent coagulopathy, prohibitive vascular access and poor candidacy for advanced heart failure therapies in the absence of myocardial recovery. Given the high rates of morbidity and mortality associated with VA-ECMO, a number of risk scores have been proposed to predict clinical outcomes when assessing a patient's candidacy for circulatory support. This decision should be made in consultation with the local multidisciplinary Shock Team and concert with the patient's health values and goals of care. Current randomized trials evaluating the clinical efficacy of VA-ECMO include ECMO-CS (NCT02301819), EUROSHOCK (NCT03813134), ECLS-SHOCK (NCT02544594) and ANCHOR (NCT04184635). Data for MCS therapy for primary RV shock following an acute inferior myocardial infarction is similarly lacking, with a single arm trial demonstrating 73% 30-day survival with Impella RP, but post-approval data in real-world practice was associated with <14% 30-day survival Both Impella RP and Protek Duo directly bypass the RV thereby, reducing right atrial (RA) pressure, while enhancing mean pulmonary arterial (PA) pressure and LV preload. In patients with RV shock with concomitant respiratory failure, VA-ECMO with consideration for LV venting may be preferred. It is reported that more than 50% of patients with AMI-CS will also sustain a cardiac arrest, either at index clinical presentation or as a complication of their deteriorating shock state. In addition, observational research has demonstrated synergisms in short and long-term mortality among patients with AMI complicated by both CS and cardiac arrest. While the Coronary Angiography after Cardiac Arrest (COACT) trial did not demonstrate a difference in 90-day survival between immediate and delayed angiography in patients with out-of-hospital CA who did not have post-resuscitative ST-segment elevation, patients with CS were excluded. Therefore, given the clinical complexities of patients with CS and cardiac arrest complicating AMI, a multidisciplinary approach is recommended in the evaluation of these patients prior to proceeding with coronary angiography, to include: 1) Vasopressor therapy, preferably with norepinephrine to achieve a viable mean arterial pressure; 2) Early mechanical ventilation to enhance tissue oxygenation and optimize acid-base status; and 3) Risk stratification using validated tools to assess the likelihood of meaningful neurologic recovery. VA-ECMO to provide circulatory support during cardiac arrest, also known as ECPR, may be considered in select patients with out-of-hospital arrest and not responsive to standard cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Recent observational data from the University of Minnesota demonstrated that despite the adverse metabolic sequelae associated with prolonged resuscitation, ECPR may be associated with improved neurologically favorable survival compared with conventional CPR for all durations of resuscitation <60 minutes (33% versus 23%; p=0.01), although mortality did increase by 25% for 10 minutes, every minute of CPR beyond 30 minutes. The decision to proceed with ECPR should be made in consultation with local Shock Team and based on criteria that take into consideration factors such as age, witnessed cardiac arrest with or without bystander CPR, presence or absence of an initial shockable rhythm and time to return of spontaneous circulation. Among resuscitated patients who remain unresponsive but are deemed clinically appropriate to proceed with coronary angiography, targeted temperature management should be implemented as soon as possible to maximize neurologic benefit. The aging of the United States population has introduced complexity in cardiovascular care for older patients with AMI. Geriatric syndromes are clinical conditions that do not fit into one disease category, but significantly increase the cardiovascular risk, morbidity, and mortality for AMI patients specifically those who suffer CS. Active search for these geriatric complexities, including frailty, multimorbidity, cognitive decline, physical dysfunction, polypharmacy, and failure to thrive, is fundamental for the decision to proceed with invasive management of AMI-CS. For AMI patients without CS, these geriatric risks are common and they predispose to increased vulnerability to stressor and complications from therapeutic interventions. Because the invasive care for AMI-CS frequently involves large bore vascular access, use of antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy, need for percutaneous revascularization, and prolonged use of mechanical support devices, the presence of preexisting geriatric syndrome may predispose to even higher degrees of mortality, disability, worsening heart failure, iatrogenesis, bleeding, and exacerbation of other preexisting medication conditions. As such, part of the invasive evaluation for AMI-CS should include a thorough evaluation of these geriatric risks, in particular advanced forms of frailty, cognitive dysfunction, and profound disability. This evaluation highlights the need for appropriate judgement in the utilization of invasive care of AMI-CS to avoid aggressive therapies that may prove futile. Integration of geriatric and palliative care consultation teams as an integral part of the standardized team-based approach to AMI-CS can supplement the decision making, risk stratification, and evaluation of futility in high risk group of older adults presenting with AMI-CS. title: Acute Myocardial Infarction and Cardiogenic Shock Interventional Approach to Management in the Cardiac Catheterization Laboratories

content: Despite the advances of noninvasive imaging modalities, the utility of pediatric cardiac catheterization in diagnostic purposes is still the gold standard investigation for many congenital heart diseases (CHDs). Echocardiography is the main non-invasive method for diagnosis of CHDs; however, it is not always sufficient for the cardiologist to assess operability or to predict the surgical outcome. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) are powerful tools used to provide anatomical and physiological information; however, their availability is not uniform at all centers. Many indications can be encountered for diagnostic cardiac catheterization (DCC). It is recommended to assess pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and reversibility of pulmonary hypertension (level of evidence: B). Recently, estimation of the pulmonary vascular resistance index (PVRI) instead has become the cornerstone for decision making for patient management according to the recent American Heart Association Guidelines (AHA). A baseline PVRI of < 6 WU m2 and a PVRI/ SVRI ratio < 0.3 have been used as an indicator of operability systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI). Also, DCC is indicated for children with complex pulmonary atresia when the data about pulmonary artery anatomy, major aorto-pulmonary collateral arteries (MAPCAs) and coronary circulation from other methods are equivocal. Meanwhile, with level of evidence C, postoperative DCC is reasonable when the early post-operative course is unexpectedly complicated and MRI and CT angiography fail to yield a clear explanation. Although diagnostic cardiac catheterization can offer valuable data about structure and hemodynamics of the underlying cardiac lesions, it should not be considered routine for diagnosis of congenital defects. Individual centers must assess their abilities for determining which catheterization cases they might perform. We were motivated to conduct this study to assess the main local indications of diagnostic catheterization in our center and the patients' clinical profile with the role of DCC in determining their managements plans. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethical Review Committee, Alexandria University on 18/May/2017 with serial number 0303637. The current study was a retrospective descriptive cross sectional study. It checked all the medical records of children catheterized by the same operator for diagnostic purposes between January 2011 and July 2012 at the cardiac catheterization laboratory of the pediatric department at Alexandria University Children's Hospital, which is considered a referral center for many hospitals. Catheter-based intervention cases were excluded. As a descriptive study it concentrated on continuous variables, i.e. variable diseases and vari-able outcomes. Hence, the sample size of the pro-posed study was 61 cases. Detailed history, clinical examinations, laboratory results and oxygen saturation data were collected. Basically, our center was lacking cardiac MRI and CT. Therefore, echocardiography was the only prior imaging modality before catheterization. Conventional echocardiography reports were analyzed for the diagnosis, cardiac function, chamber dilatations, coronaries anomalies and pressure gradients specially across tricuspid and pulmonary valves whether for regurgitations or stenosis. The machine was a Madison 990 (2 and 5 MHz transducers). It was performed at the pediatric cardiac catheterization unit. Before the procedure, the patients and their relatives were emotionally prepared and informed consent forms were signed. Children were kept fasting for 4-5 h except for regularly scheduled oral medications. At the time of the procedure, general anesthesia was induced by intravenous administration of propofol and ketamine, then it was maintained by inhalation of halothane. Venous and arterial access were obtained after puncturing femoral vessels by the Seldinger technique. After advancement of sheath and dilators (no. 5-6 Fr) heparin (100 U/kg) was given at the beginning of the procedure. NIH catheters were the usual used catheters for right heart catheterization while a pigtail catheter was used for the left side of the heart. A complete profile of the hemodynamic state of the heart was assessed including pressures and obtaining samples for blood gases. Different cineangiographic pictures were recorded in anteroposterior and lateral views (biplane projection) after injection of non-ionic contrast material (Omnipaque) from a flow injector (1 ml/kg) at a rate of 1 ml/s. After the procedure children were given antibiotics as a routine prophylactic measure and monitored for the next 12 h then discharged. The reports were checked to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate hemodynamic data as mean pulmonary artery pressure (PAP), PVR, systemic vascular resistance (SVR), PVRI, PVRI/SVRI and Qp : Qs (ratio of arterial pulmonary flow to systemic blood flow). The reference values of these parameters were checked according to AHA guidelines. Also, cineangiographic pictures were analyzed to assess chamber size, obstructive lesions, shunts, MAPCAs and coronaries anomalies and to calculate McGoon's ratio for tetralogy of Fallot cases. It was calculated by dividing the sum of the diameters of right pulmonary artery (RPA) and left pulmonary artery (LPA) by the diameter of the aorta at the level above the diaphragm (RPA + LPA/AO)). An average value of 2.1 was noted in normal subjects. A ratio above 1.2 is associated with acceptable postoperative RV systolic pressure in tetralogy of Fallot. A ratio below 0.8 is deemed inadequate for complete repair of pulmonary atresia cases with TOF anatomy (TOF/PA). Data were fed to the computer and analyzed using IBM SPSS software package version 20.0. Comparisons between groups for categorical variables were assessed using the chi2 test. The Mann-Whitney test was used to compare two groups for abnormally distributed quantitative variables. Student's t-test was used for normally distributed quantitative variables, to compare between two studied groups. Significance of the obtained results was judged at the 5% level. Qualitative data were described using number and percent, while normally quantitative data were expressed as mean +- SD, and abnormally distributed data were expressed as median (min.-max.). The medical records of 61 children subjected to DCC were checked and included in the study. Patients' ages ranged from 4 month to 144 months (median: 26 months). The enrolled cases were categorized into 2 main groups: group I (n = 25) included cases suffering from pulmonary hypertension with intracardiac shunts based on clinical and echocardiographic diagnosis; and group II (n = 36) included children suffering from different forms of obstructive pulmonary diseases with or without cyanosis, as summarized in Table I. Ventricular septal defects (VSD) were the most common diagnosis (60%) among GI, especially the perimembranous type, while tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) was the most frequent diagnosis among GII (55.5%). However, TOF cases were predominant among the studied patients (27.2%) (Table I). The majority of patients included in GI were be-tween 1 and 2 years of age and of VSD type while below 1 year the cases varied between VSD and TGA/VSD (transposition of great arteries). Cases above 4 years (12%) were mostly suffering from TOF or complete atrioventricular septal defects (CAVCDs). Mostly oxygen saturation (O2 sat) for GI patients ranged from 78% to 98%, as shown in Table II. It was below 85% in 12% (n = 3 cases). Three patients were confirmed to be Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Echocardiography estimated the pressure gradient of tricuspid and pulmonary regurgitation (PGTR and PGPR) for 17 cases among group I with mean 40 +-10.8 and 29.7 +-7.5 respectively, as summarized in Table III. Cardiac catheterization hemodynamic data of GI after giving 100% oxygen (vaso-reactivity test - VRT) were summarized in Table III. The mean of PAP was 46.4 +-15.4. However, 2 cases had a mean PAP of less than 25 mm Hg. The pulmonary to systemic blood flow ratio (Qp : Qs) had a mean of 1.74 +-0.80 for all GI patients; Qp : Qs was > 3 for 2 patients, Qp : Qs ranged from 2 to 3 for 10 cases, > 1 for 7 cases and Qp : Qs = 1 for 2 cases. The PVRI had a wide range from 0.42 to 9.17 with a median of 0.93. Also, the PVRI/SVRI ranged from 0.11 to 0.91 with a median of 0.25. About 84% of cases (n = 21) had PVRI < 6 WU m2 and PVRI/SVRI < 0.3, while 1 (4%) case remained with PVRI; 9.16 WU m2 and PVRI/SVRI; 0.91. Three (12%) cases had PVRI/SVRI > 0.3; (0.86, 0.48, 0.39 respectively) but the PVRI was < 6 WU m2. After analysis of catheterization reports and according to the AHA guidelines the patients' management plans ranged between operable conditions, inoperable cases and cases recommended for sildenafil therapy as summarized in Table IV. Comparing the demographic, echocardiographic and catheterization data of the operable and non-operable subgroups revealed a statistically significant difference between the two subgroups in age as the inoperable group included older children (median: 57 vs. 24, p = 0.014). Echocardiography showed a significant difference for higher PGPR for non-operable when compared to operable patients (36.3 +-8.5 vs. 28.2 +-6.6, p = 0.049) as summarized in Table III. The mean of PVR, PVRI, PVRI/SVRI, RV and PAP pressures were higher for non-operable cases (GI-B) when compared to operable subgroup GI-A with significant difference. Meanwhile, Qp : Qs results were significantly lower for non-operable cases (< 1) when compared to the operable subgroup, as summarized in Table III. On the other hand, GII included patients with obstructive pulmonary artery defects. About 33.3% of the cases were above 4 years and the diagnosis varied between classic TOF, PS/ASD, PS/VSD and DCRV. Meanwhile 19.2% were below one year with different diagnosis as TGA/PS, TOF/PA and PS with left pulmonary branch ostial stenosis and with O sat below 87% (Tables I and II). After checking cineangiographic pictures, the McGoon ratio was calculated for all TOF cases as a predictor of operability. It ranged from 0.7 to 3.2 (median: 1.8); 8 cases had a ratio below 1.8. Table IV summarized the patients' outcome of GII for different plans (operable, palliative shunt or stenting before operation). Comparing the management plans for GII cases based only on echocardiographic findings to the plans based on cardiac catheterization resulted in some matched and unmatched cases for every diagnosis, as summarized in Table V. There was a statistically significant difference between matched/unmatched plans based on echocardiography and catheterization concerned for TOF/PA cases (chi2 = 7.438, p = 0.023). Whereas, other CHDs included in GII there were no significant difference between the matched and unmatched reports of echocardiography and catheterizations. Advances in cardiac care worldwide have allowed the repair of CHDs to take place from infancy or even during the neonatal period for many patients, before the development of complications. However, in developing countries the surgical management of a lot of cases becomes delayed to childhood as they have no access to cardiovascular care. Although the utility of diagnostic cardiac catheterization in the clinical setting has diminished over the last years, is still constitutes a valuable tool in some aspects in the workup of CHDs, especially for older children. The current study focused on studying the local indications of DCC at our center in order to reflect the impact of that on our patients' management. It is important to point out that our center lacked CT and MRI; echocardiography was the only available non-invasive imaging method. In our study, medical files of 61 patients were revised and grouped into a PH group and obstructive pulmonary artery disease group. The PH group included a spectrum of diseases. VSD cases were the predominant defect among the shunt group, similar to the conclusion of Saxena et al., and also matched with an Egyptian study performed at Alexandria which stated the same, and it considered other shunts, ASD, PDA, CAVC and TGA, less common. Meanwhile, TOF was the most common indication among the obstructive pulmonary bed group and was the most common diagnosis among the whole study group (27.2% TOF vs. 24.5%, VSD). However, that was inconsistent with Kumar, who found the ratio of TOF to VSD to be 1 : 3, and this may be attributed to delayed surgical correction of TOF cases in our country when compared to VSD cases. This may be explained by the complex anatomy of TOF, requiring more skilled surgeons and better postoperative care. It was clearly evident through comparing the main age group of both cases at the time of DCC (> 4 years for GII versus 1-2 years for GI). In our study, PH was documented by DCC for all cases except for 2 of them (6.6%). The reports showed mean PAP < 25 mm Hg after the vasoreactivity test and normal PVRI values which declared that they were not good candidates for DCC from the start. This was consistent with Groh et al., who reported that echocardiography inaccurately estimates right ventricular pressure in children, either overestimating or underestimating it. Another meta-analysis study showed that pooled sensitivity and specificity of Doppler echocardiography for the diagnosis of PH were 88% and 56%. However, this was contradictory to Sohrabi et al., who found a significant correlation between systolic PAP by catheterization and TR velocity by echocardiography with sensitivity 92.8% and specificity of 86.6%. Therefore, although echo inaccurately estimates PH, it still has acceptable specificity and sensitivity in detecting severe PH. Those 2 patients had mild PH and also their ages were 6 and 8 months, with large VSD, which raised the value of the suggestion from the Taleb study; rare and remote possibility of elevated PVR below 1 year of age. This will be considered in our further indications for DCC to overcome unnecessary use. After checking the hemodynamic data of the PH group, the plans of management were classified according to recent AHA guidelines into operable (84%) and non-operable (16%) (inoperable (4%) and borderline inoperable (sildenafil therapy) (12%) for 6 months then reassessment). Comparing the clinical profile of operable and non-operable subgroups revealed that the difference in the age of patients was significant among both, as operable children were younger, around 24 months, while non-operable children were older, around 57 months. Therefore, older patients > 2 years may have higher risk for inoperability than younger ones, which mandates the indication of DCC prior to surgical corrections for better prediction of surgical outcome. Moreover, pressure gradient values of pulmonary regurgitation were significantly higher among the non-operable group, while pressure gradient values of tricuspid regurgitation showed no significant difference between the two groups, in disagreement with Sohrabi et al. maybe because of the small sample size. Concerning the catheterization hemodynamic parameters, PVRI and resistance ratio were significantly higher for the non-operable group compared to the operable group. One case was inoperable (Eisenmenger syndrome); Down syn-drome, 6 years and half, wide outlet type VSD, no history of prior pulmonary artery banding, PVRI = 9.2 and resistance ratio = 0.7. Whereas the other 3 cases with borderline/inoperability were recommended for sildenafil treatment for 6 months then reassessment. The other patients were recommended for elective corrective surgery with a predicted favorable outcome. Concerning group II, the obstructive PA group, TOF represented more than half the cases. The surgical repair strategy was dependent on ensuring adequate PA size and distal pulmonary vascular bed with exclusion of coronary anomalies and MAPCAs, for which there is considered limited ability by echocardiography, especially in older children and obese patients. Furthermore, echocardiography ability is better at assessing the right pulmonary artery branch than the left. This may be because the left pulmonary artery's posterior course is poorly visualized via transthoracic scanning view. The McGoon ratio is a reliable parameter in predicting the operability of TOF as it is proportionate to pulmonary flow and considered a goal for DCC. Some studies admitted the useful role of MRI in calculating the McGoon ratio non-invasively. However, it takes a long time to perform MRI, needs fully cooperative or sedated subjects, produces a poorer quality image in cases of severe cardiac arrhythmia, is expensive and requires expertise in image acquisition. Computed tomography has become capable of delineating the anatomy in multiple planes within 2 min, with less radiation, especially in older patients, although some studies stated false positive data about MAPCAs. As long as these modalities were not available, we were obliged to perform DCC for all TOF cases, even classic and those younger than 1 year. After revising the DCC reports, the patients' management plans and operability were determined for GII according to each CHD's pre-requisites for intervention. About 60% of cases of TOF were classic and had a McGoon ratio > 1.8 and were recommended for surgical correction as recommended by many studies for a favorable surgical outcome. However, the other 40% of TOF had either hypoplastic pulmonary vascular beds or significant MAPCS collaterals and the diagnosis varied between TOF/PA and classic TOF in older children (> 4 years), which affected their management plans between shunt or intervention for the collateral. Our results matched the Kumar study in India, which found MAPCS in older children with classic TOF and recommended DCC in absence of CT or MRI before corrective surgery. Stent dilation were recommended for PS/LPA stenosis. All cases of VSD/PS were operable as they had normal hemodynamics as pulmonary stenosis decreased the overwork over the right ventricle similar to pulmonary artery banding. It was interesting to compare the matching or non-matching between the echocardiography and cardiac angiography reports for operable and inoperable subgroups II. It highlighted the superior role of DCC over echocardiography in certain conditions and the unnecessary indications of DCC for others. Concerning cases of TOF/PA, they had significantly unmatched echocardiography reports when compared to DCC, which mandates the DCC. This agreed with recommended guidelines and many studies. Meanwhile, for classic TOF, VSD/PS, PS/LPA, TGA/PS and DCRV reports did not show a significant difference in matched and unmatched criteria to catheterization reports between operable and non-operable groups. Results of TGS/PS and DCRV cases were based on small samples (1 case each) so it deserves further studies on larger samples. Apart from classic TOF cases especially older children and PS cases specially with LPAs, all cases of VSD/PS were unnecessarily catheterized as long as the echocardiographic report showed left to right shunt at rest and exercise. For our local center diagnostic cardiac cauterization had a positive contribution in decision making in medical or surgical management for about 85.2% of the indicated cases; however, about 14.8% of cases had no added benefits. This agreed with a similar Indian study conducted to assess the role of DCC in the patient's fate and had almost the same logistics of developing countries; they concluded the great importance for DCC in further management of over than 90% of their pediatric cases. Also, it agreed with other studies in Pakistan and Sudan. In conclusion, the diagnostic role of pediatric cardiac catheterization remains the "final authority" for definitive anatomic and hemodynamic information. However, the utility and the indications should be adjusted according to the local circumstances of every center in order to achieve the maximum positive contribution for patients' management plans.

title: The role of diagnostic cardiac catheterization for children with congenital heart diseases: local experience
